title: Introduction to sociology: society, inequality and change
summary: This course introduces undergraduates to how sociologists see and study social life. Students learn core theories and research methods, then apply them to culture, socialization, class, race, gender, family, education, deviance and social change. Two analysis papers, a midterm and a final exam assess their work.
brief: Introduction to Sociology for undergraduates: 15 weeks, two 75-minute class meetings a week with about 40 students. The sociological imagination, research methods, culture and socialization, social class and inequality, race and ethnicity, gender, family, education, deviance and social change. Textbook: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e. Reading quizzes at the start of most classes 15%, two short analysis papers 15% each, a midterm 20%, a final exam 25%, participation in discussion 10%.
setup: Reading quizzes at the start of most classes

l_270e8f3e4a4f.title: The sociological imagination
l_270e8f3e4a4f.summary: Students learn C. Wright Mills's idea of linking personal troubles to public issues, and set out how participation in discussion is judged.
readings: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e, ch. 1 (to confirm) (An Introduction to Sociology)

slides.title: The sociological imagination
bullets: Introduction to sociology: society, inequality and change
Textbook: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e
Today: personal troubles, public issues and the discussion
slides.notes: Welcome the class. About 40 students, and for most this is the first sociology course. Nothing today relies on reading or preparation beforehand. Reading quizzes at the start of most classes begin next time, and you will say so on the last slide. Introduce yourself, the textbook and how the class runs. Then move to the opening question on the next slide.

slides.title: What sociologists ask
bullets: Sociology studies society and social behavior
Private lives follow patterns shared by many people
C. Wright Mills named the habit of seeing this
The Sociological Imagination (Mills, 1959)
Today: troubles, issues and three shaping forces
slides.notes: Open with a question to the whole room and take three or four answers: why did you enroll in college this fall? List the answers on the board in two columns without comment, one for personal reasons (interest, family expectations, a career goal) and one for wider reasons (cost of living, employers asking for degrees, scholarships, what peers did). Point out that nearly every answer mixes the two. That is Mills’s point. His book, The Sociological Imagination (New York: Oxford University Press, 1959), argues that people often feel their lives as private problems when they are tied to the larger society. Keep this brief. The OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, ch. 1 introduces the idea, and students were asked to read it. Do not assume they did. Explain the idea in your own words. Do not quote Mills.

slides.title: Participation in discussion
bullets: Counts 10% of the course grade
Scored in class, as it happens
Your own work, scored on your own contribution
Scoring starts with today’s discussion
Nothing to hand in
slides.notes: Say how this piece works in your own words. The instructions for Participation in discussion are yours to give, so state them here as you have set them. Tell students that today’s group discussion is the first time it is scored, and that nothing was expected of them beforehand. Tell students what you will be listening for, as you have written it. Invite questions about the format before moving on. Explain also that reading quizzes at the start of most classes begin next time and are a separate component, 15% of the course grade.

slides.title: Personal trouble or public issue
bullets: Unemployment: one worker, or millions
Mills: the same event can be both
slides.notes: Teach this with short exposition, about ten minutes, then check understanding by asking a few students to restate the difference in their own words. Mills defined personal troubles as matters in an individual’s character and close relationships, and public issues as matters that reach beyond the individual to the institutions of a society. His own illustration was unemployment: when one person in a small city is out of work, we look to that person’s skills, habits and choices. When millions in a nation are out of work, no one can explain it by the character of each individual, and the economy itself is in question. Paraphrase this and do not quote Mills. Read down the table row by row. Stress that the table gives two lenses, not two kinds of events. The same job loss can be seen through either, and the sociological imagination moves between them. Take one or two student questions, then explain the group task on the next slide.

slides.title: Group discussion: one factory closing
bullets: Suppose a toy factory in a town of 20,000 closes. 1,500 workers lose their jobs. This case is hypothetical.
1. Maria is one of the 1,500. Give two explanations of her job loss that point to Maria, and two that point to the economy.
2. Suppose only Maria had lost her job and the factory stayed open. What changes when 1,500 lose theirs at once?
3. Name one remedy that fits a personal trouble and one that fits a public issue.
Groups of four. Every member speaks to every question.
slides.notes:
This is the Participation in discussion for today. Form groups of four, ten groups, and ask them to turn their chairs together. Give the instructions as you have set them. Allow about twelve minutes. Within each group every student answers; suggest that each member opens one question and the others respond, so that all four are heard. Circulate and listen, and score each student on their own contribution as it happens. Do not show or read the answers below until the discussion is finished.

Answers for your reference.
Question 1. Explanations pointing to Maria: she lacked a skill the employer wanted, she did not look for another job early enough, she chose a job in one industry, she did not save money. Explanations pointing to the economy: the owner moved production elsewhere, foreign or automated production lowered costs, demand for the product fell, the town depended on one employer.
Question 2. If only Maria lost her job, her personal traits and decisions are the natural explanation, so it is a personal trouble. When 1,500 lose theirs, that is 7.5 percent of the town’s population (1,500 divided by 20,000), and the cause cannot lie in 1,500 separate characters. Shops lose customers, the school district and town lose tax revenue, and housing prices may fall. This is a public issue.
Question 3. Personal trouble: Maria improves her résumé, applies widely, retrains on her own or moves. Public issue: job training funded by government, unemployment insurance, attracting new employers, policy on plant closings, diversifying the local economy.

Debrief with the whole class for about ten minutes. Ask one group to give its answer to question 2 and ask others to add or disagree. Write on the board where the answer sits: person or society. Conclude that Maria faces a personal trouble for her, and the town faces a public issue.

slides.title: History, biography and social structure
bullets: Biography: one person’s life, choices and background
History: the period and its events
Social structure: institutions, roles, patterned relationships
The imagination links all three
slides.notes: Explain, in your own words, that Mills asked three questions of any society: what is its structure, where does it stand in history, and what kinds of people does it produce. Present the three terms as a working tool. Apply them to Maria. Biography: her education, skills and age. History: the period in which the plant closes, for instance whether the national economy is growing or in recession. Structure: the town’s economy, the labor market and the laws about work. Then ask students to turn to a neighbor for two minutes and apply the three terms to a different case: a student who cannot afford tuition. Take two or three answers. Point out that a good answer names all three, not only the person. Refer students to OpenStax 3e, ch. 1, on the sociological imagination for the textbook version.

slides.title: History shapes the odds of finding work
bullets: Same skills, different years, different odds
Biography alone cannot explain these shifts
slides.notes: Show the chart. The figures are the annual average U.S. unemployment rate from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, in percent of the labor force: 2008, 5.8; 2010, 9.6; 2012, 8.1; 2014, 6.2; 2016, 4.9; 2018, 3.9; 2020, 8.1. These are real figures. Ask: a graduate with the same skills looks for work in 2010 and again in 2018. What differs? Draw out that the person is the same and the period differs. History changed the odds. Link back to the three terms: biography is the graduate, history is the year, and structure is the labor market that moves the rate. Then make the point of the lesson: when the rate is this high, unemployment is a public issue, not only a personal trouble. Finish by asking each student to write one sentence to a neighbor that uses the words trouble and issue about their own life. Take two volunteers.

slides.title: Founders and theoretical perspectives
bullets: Functionalism, conflict theory, symbolic interactionism
Durkheim, Marx, Weber, Mead
One institution, three lenses: the school
slides.notes: Welcome students and move straight to the reading quiz. Today each student states the central claim of the three perspectives and then applies all three to one institution, the school. The discussion in the third segment is where participation is scored.

slides.title: Reading quiz: theoretical perspectives
bullets: Reading: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e, chapter 1 (to confirm)
Section: theoretical perspectives in sociology
Marked in points
Part of Reading quizzes (15%)
Work alone and in silence
slides.notes: The quiz is the teacher’s own paper, with its questions, key and points. Give the conditions in your own words, including what students may bring or use. Collect or close the quiz in whatever way you have announced, then take a short moment to settle the room before the exposition. Keep the screen on this slide while students work; no answers are shown.

slides.title: Four founders, four ideas
bullets: Durkheim: social facts, solidarity, anomie
Marx: class struggle over the means of production
Weber: rationalization, verstehen, class, status and power
Mead: the self arises through taking the role of others
slides.notes: Keep this brief and ask students to add detail from the reading. Durkheim: social facts are patterns that shape individuals from outside (Suicide, 1897); he contrasted mechanical and organic solidarity (The Division of Labor in Society, 1893) and used anomie for a loss of clear norms. Marx: with Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848); owners of the means of production (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat) have opposed interests. Weber: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) and rationalization, the spread of efficiency and calculation, as in bureaucracy; verstehen, interpretive understanding of the meaning people attach to action; and his three dimensions of stratification. Weber links conflict theory and interactionism, so note that he does not belong neatly to one camp. Mead: Mind, Self, and Society (1934), assembled by his students after his death; the self develops through play, games and the generalized other. Ask: which of these four ideas did you find hardest in the chapter?

slides.title: Three perspectives compared
bullets: Weber’s work informs both conflict theory and interactionism
slides.notes: Students should be able to state each central claim in one sentence. Functionalism: social institutions persist because they serve functions for the whole; Merton’s distinction between manifest and latent functions comes from the reading. Conflict theory: society is shaped by competition over scarce resources, and order is often imposed by the powerful. Symbolic interactionism: a micro-level view in which people act toward things on the basis of shared meanings, and Herbert Blumer named it. Point out the level of analysis: the first two are macro-level, the third micro-level. Ask two students to restate one row without looking at the screen. Then explain that in the next segment the class applies all three to the school, and that students lead the discussion.

rows: What does each part do for stability?
What do people take things to mean?

slides.title: Discussion: one school, three lenses
bullets: Functionalist: name one manifest and one latent function of a US high school.
Conflict: many states fund public schools partly through local property taxes. What would a conflict theorist say about this?
Interactionist: a teacher labels a student as gifted. How might that meaning shape what happens next?
slides.notes:
Participation in discussion (10%) is scored as it happens; the instructions for it are the teacher’s to give. Students lead; speak only to redirect. Take the questions in order, with a few minutes on each and students calling on one another.

Question 1, answers to listen for: manifest functions are the intended ones, such as teaching literacy, mathematics and civic knowledge, and certifying completion. Latent functions are unintended, such as childcare that frees parents to work, building peer networks, and a place where young people meet future partners. Durkheim’s idea that schools teach shared norms and prepare children for roles fits here.

Question 2, answers to listen for: districts with higher property values raise more money, so schools in wealthier areas often spend more per student. A conflict theorist reads this as one way advantage is passed on across generations, as groups with more resources secure better schooling. Push students to name who benefits and who loses.

Question 3, answers to listen for: the label becomes a shared definition of the situation. The teacher may call on the student more, offer harder work and praise effort. The student may then see himself or herself as capable, which is Mead’s point about the self formed through others’ views. Rosenthal and Jacobson’s 1968 study, Pygmalion in the Classroom, is a well-known source on teacher expectations if a student asks.

slides.title: A student stops attending school. What would each perspective ask first?
bullets: Functionalist: what would you ask?
Conflict theorist: what would you ask?
Interactionist: what would you ask?
Which question would you pursue first, and why?
slides.notes: Participation in discussion continues; students lead and answer one another. Answers to listen for: a functionalist asks whether the school and its connected institutions, such as family and community, are integrating the student, and Durkheim’s anomie can enter if ties and expectations are weak. A conflict theorist asks about resources: school funding, tracking, the student’s family income, and whether the school serves some groups better than others. An interactionist asks how the student and the teachers define each other and the situation, including labeling, and what attending or leaving means to the student. Weber is useful for pressing further: ask whether a rule-bound bureaucratic school treats the student as a case rather than a person. Do not settle on a single winner; the strongest contributions explain what the chosen perspective leaves out.

slides.title: What each lens sees, and what it misses
bullets: Pick the perspective that fits your question, and name its limits
slides.notes: Synthesis. Draw on what students said in the discussion and attach their points to the rows. The takeaway: the perspectives are not rival answers to one question but different questions about the same institution, and a good analysis names which one it is using and why. This habit matters for the analysis papers later in the course, which are graded separately as Short analysis paper 1 (15%) and Short analysis paper 2 (15%); the teacher gives their instructions when they are set. Close by asking each student to say, in a sentence, the central claim of the perspective they found most persuasive today.

readings: OpenStax, Introduction to Sociology 3e, ch. 20 (to confirm) (Population, Urbanization, and the Environment)

l_62e5f294c44e.title: Review for the final exam
l_62e5f294c44e.summary: Students review the whole course through practice questions on inequality, institutions, deviance and change; the final exam is sat afterwards.

descriptors.x_984585b8d5f4: Applies relevant sociological concepts accurately and develops a clear explanation of how social relationships, institutions or historical conditions shape the situation.

descriptors.x_c3576ca0079a: Uses a relevant sociological concept but applies it partly inaccurately or leaves its connection to the situation unclear.
descriptors.x_875d27f5dcb0: Offers an unsupported label or personal opinion without a meaningful application of relevant sociological concepts.

descriptors.x_984585b8d5f4: Supports claims with specific relevant details, clearly distinguishes evidence from assumptions, and explains what further information would resolve uncertainty.
